intro: Every copy of the Tanakh you can hold is the end of a chain. A scribe copied it from a copy, which was copied from a copy, back through printing presses in Venice, codices in Tiberias and Cairo, scrolls in caves by the Dead Sea, and manuscripts nobody has seen for two thousand years. Along the way the text was translated into Greek, Aramaic, Latin, German and English, and each translation made choices the reader cannot see. This unit follows that chain link by link.

The questions are practical ones that any careful reader can ask. What did the oldest copies say, and how do we know? Who added the vowels to a text written in consonants? Why does the Greek Jeremiah differ from the Hebrew? What did the JPS committee of 1917 decide about Isaiah 7:14, and why did the King James decide otherwise? What happens to a word like chesed when it becomes mercy? Jewish tradition holds the text as received; historians trace how it was received; translators sit in between. This unit lets you hear all three.

By the end you will be able to name the main witnesses to the Hebrew text and place them in order, explain what the Masoretes did and why it mattered, read a famous variant and weigh it, set two translations of one verse side by side and say what each translator chose, and explain why Jews write the LORD for the name of God. You will also have a habit: when you read a verse in English, you will ask who translated it, when, for whom, and from what.
bigQuestion: How did the words of the Tanakh reach us, and what does it mean to read them in translation?

timeline.t: The Torah is translated into Greek in Alexandria; the Septuagint begins
The Great Isaiah Scroll is copied; it will lie in a cave at Qumran for two thousand years
One form of the Hebrew text becomes standard among Jews; the Aramaic Targums take shape
The Masoretes of Tiberias fix vowels, accents and the masorah
The Aleppo Codex is written and vocalized by Aaron ben Asher
The Leningrad Codex, the oldest complete Masoretic Bible, is finished in Cairo
Bomberg prints the second Rabbinic Bible in Venice, edited by Jacob ben Hayyim
The King James Version is published in England
The Jewish Publication Society publishes its English Tanakh, edited by Max Margolis
Buber and Rosenzweig translate the Bible into German; Buber finishes alone
The first Dead Sea Scrolls are found; the Aleppo Codex is damaged in riots
The complete NJPS Tanakh appears; Fox's Five Books follows in 1995 and Alter's Bible in 2018

words.d: ancient manuscripts found from 1947 on near Qumran, including the oldest known copies of books of the Tanakh
the Greek translation of the Tanakh begun in Alexandria around the third century BCE; abbreviated LXX
an Aramaic translation of a biblical book, grown from verse-by-verse translation in the synagogue
Jewish scholars, chiefly of Tiberias, c. 7th–10th centuries CE, who fixed the vowels, accents and notes of the Hebrew text
the standard Hebrew text of the Tanakh as fixed by the Masoretes; the text of every synagogue scroll and Jewish translation
a book of bound pages, as opposed to a scroll; the form of the Aleppo and Leningrad Bibles
what is written and what is read: places where the Masoretes kept the written consonants but marked a different word to say aloud
the study of manuscripts and versions to trace a text's transmission and its earliest recoverable form
Hebrew for a young woman of marriageable age; the word at Isaiah 7:14 that JPS 1917 renders the young woman and the King James a virgin
loyal, active kindness within a bond; rendered mercy, kindness or lovingkindness in JPS 1917
translated sense for sense into natural English, as NJPS does, rather than word for word
my Lord: the word Jews say in place of the four-letter name of God, which translations render the LORD

test.q: What makes the Dead Sea Scrolls important for the text of the Tanakh?
choices: They are the only copies written by the prophets themselves
They are about a thousand years older than the oldest complete Hebrew Bibles known before
They contain the vowels the Masoretes later removed
test.why: The scrolls date from about the third century BCE to the first century CE, far older than the tenth- and eleventh-century codices.

test.q: Which book of the Tanakh does the Great Isaiah Scroll contain, and how much of it?
test.why: The Great Isaiah Scroll holds the complete book of Isaiah in 54 columns.

test.q: Where and roughly when was the Septuagint begun?
test.why: Tradition places the Greek Torah in Alexandria under Ptolemy II, around 250 BCE.

test.q: What is the Letter of Aristeas?
choices: A letter from Rashi to a student
The preface of the JPS 1917 translation
A Greek text telling the legend of seventy-two translators
test.why: The Letter of Aristeas tells how seventy-two elders produced the Greek Torah for King Ptolemy; the name Septuagint comes from it.

test.q: Which of these differs between the Samaritan Pentateuch and the Masoretic Text at Deuteronomy 27:4?
choices: The name of the mountain: Gerizim or Ebal
The number of commandments: nine or ten
The name of the prophet: Moses or Joshua
test.why: The Samaritan text places the altar on Gerizim, its holy mountain; the Masoretic Text reads Ebal.

test.q: What did the Masoretes of Tiberias add to the Hebrew text?
choices: Vowel points, cantillation accents and marginal notes
test.why: The Masoretes fixed pronunciation with vowel points, chanting with accents, and guarded the text with the masorah.

choices: The Aramaic Targum on the Torah
The rule that the harder reading is older
The body of notes counting letters, words and forms to guard the text
The order of books in the Tanakh
test.why: The masorah is the Masoretes' apparatus of notes and counts, written in the margins of the codices.

test.q: Which codex was damaged in Aleppo in 1947 and lost most of its Torah?
choices: The Cairo Codex of the Prophets
test.why: The Aleppo Codex survived the December 1947 riots but lost about a third of its pages; the Leningrad Codex is complete.

test.q: On which manuscript are the Biblia Hebraica editions based?
test.why: Biblia Hebraica has printed the Leningrad Codex since 1937; the Hebrew University Bible Project uses the Aleppo Codex.

test.q: What does the rule of the harder reading say?
choices: The longest reading is always right
The more difficult reading is often older, because copyists smooth rather than roughen
The reading in the most manuscripts is always right
The Masoretic Text is always right
test.why: Copyists tend to ease difficulties, so a harder reading is less likely to be a later change; the rule is a guide, not a law.

test.q: How does JPS 1917 render Isaiah 7:14, and how does the King James?
choices: JPS the young woman; KJV a virgin
JPS a virgin; KJV the young woman
test.why: JPS 1917 renders the Hebrew almah; the King James follows the Greek parthenos.

test.q: Who was the editor-in-chief of the JPS 1917 translation?
test.why: Margolis led the 1917 committee; Orlinsky led the NJPS Torah, Leeser translated in 1853, and Buber worked in German.

test.q: Which translation aims to make the target language sound like Hebrew, keeping repeated words and breath-length lines?
choices: Buber and Rosenzweig's German, and Fox's English after it
test.why: Buber, Rosenzweig and Fox translate for the ear, keeping Hebrew word order, repetition and line units.

test.q: What does nefesh most often mean in the Tanakh?
test.why: Nefesh is the living creature, its breath and hunger; ruach is wind or spirit, shalom peace, torah teaching.

test.q: When an English Bible prints the LORD in small capitals, what does the Hebrew have?
test.why: Small-capital LORD marks the four-letter name, which Jews read as Adonai; God usually renders Elohim.

write.prompt: Choose one verse from this unit (Genesis 1:1–2, Isaiah 7:14, Deuteronomy 32:8, Micah 6:8 or Psalm 19:8). Set out what the Hebrew says, what two witnesses or translations (such as the Masoretic Text and the Septuagint, or JPS 1917 and the King James) do with it, and how Jewish and other readers have read the result. Then argue: what must a reader of English know to read this verse fairly?
tips: Name the text you cite: book, chapter and verse, and the translation and its year.
Attribute every reading: Jewish tradition holds, the Septuagint renders, the JPS committee chose, Rashi reads.
Compare rather than judge: show what each translator or copyist valued, not which one is right.
Use the unit's terms where they fit: witness, variant, Masoretic Text, almah, chesed, idiomatic.
End with the habit: who translated, when, for whom and from what.
